title: Design an Offline Social Insight Platform
prompt:
Design an offline analytics platform that turns customer-provided social-content archives into searchable engagement and audience insights. The platform receives immutable data manifests and files that contain accounts, posts, interactions, and periodic metric snapshots. It must validate data, ingest each logical record once despite retries, build daily aggregates, and expose a queryable report after an import completes.

Do not rely on direct scraping or a third-party service API. State the import contract, durable records, ingestion flow, retry and pacing strategy, tenant isolation, correction policy for revised archives, and the reliability and analytics metrics you would operate. Assume large historical backfills and many concurrent tenants, but not an interactive real-time feed.

response.placeholder: Define the supplied-data contract and completion semantics first. Then trace a manifest from validation through idempotent ingestion, offline aggregation, and report publication.
response.reference_answer:
## 1. Scope and success condition

The system consumes customer-provided immutable archives rather than fetching from an external network. An import is successful when its manifest is durably accepted, every valid record is either written once or recorded as rejected with a reason, required aggregates are materialized, and a versioned report is published. This separates ingestion acknowledgement from analytics completion.

## 2. Import contract and durable state

`POST /imports` accepts a tenant ID, archive manifest, schema version, snapshot period, and client idempotency key. The manifest lists immutable object names, checksums, record counts when available, and a source revision. The control database stores an import record, file state, validation errors, progress counters, and report version. A unique `(tenant_id, client_key)` returns the same import on retry; each normalized record has a durable identity such as `(tenant_id, dataset_id, record_type, source_record_id, revision)`.

## 3. Reliable offline pipeline

A gateway verifies manifest shape, object ownership, size limits, checksums, and schema compatibility before queuing file work. Workers parse files in bounded chunks, validate required fields and timestamp ranges, normalize records into append-only storage, and write an outbox event in the same transaction. A batch coordinator consumes completed partitions, produces daily account and content aggregates, and publishes a report pointer only after the expected partition set reaches a terminal state. Invalid records go to a quarantined error table with a code and sample-safe diagnostics instead of blocking unrelated valid data.

## 4. Idempotency, retries, and pacing

The database uniqueness constraint is the final duplicate barrier; workers treat unique-key conflicts for the same logical payload as successful replays. File and partition state use leases and attempt IDs, so a crashed worker can be retried without two workers publishing the same completion. Retry only transient failures, use exponential backoff with jitter, cap attempts, and send permanently malformed files to review.

A scheduler enforces tenant concurrency, bytes-in-flight, storage-write, and aggregation budgets. It admits backfills gradually and keeps a separate small queue for correction work so one huge import cannot monopolize the pipeline. These are internal pacing controls, not assumptions about a third-party request limit.

## 5. Revisions, privacy, and operations

A revised archive creates a new dataset revision. The system compares record identities and either applies an idempotent upsert plus affected-day recomputation or rebuilds the affected tenant partition, depending on correction volume. Reports name the revision and coverage period so users do not mistake partial data for final results. Tenant-scoped encryption, access checks, retention controls, and redacted diagnostics protect archive contents.

I would monitor validation-failure rate, duplicate-replay rate, lease expiry, queue age, bytes and records processed, per-stage retry rate, aggregation lag, report freshness, correction backlog, and cost per completed import. A useful SLO is a percentile time from accepted manifest to published report, segmented by archive size and tenant class.
